I’ve been working this 1.5 mu plot in Quzhou for twenty years. With six people at home and some of the younger ones working off-farm in the county town, I can’t be out here all day, but this land is still the backbone of our grain supply. In the North China Plain, the only sensible system for a small plot like mine is wheat-maize double cropping — I use every inch twice a year.

For **winter wheat**, I’ll sow an improved local variety in early October after rotary tilling the whole field. I know this soil, so I’ll put down compound fertilizer as a base and topdress urea at green-up in spring. Water from my well is reliable; I’ll irrigate three times — before winter dormancy, at jointing when the wheat shoots up, and once more at grain filling. I’ll spray twice: a herbicide in early spring and a fungicide or insecticide if the weather turns damp and disease shows up. I expect about 900 jin per mu, which is what this land usually gives me if the spring rains don’t fail.

Right after harvesting wheat in mid-June, I need to move fast. I’ll plant **hybrid maize** — everyone uses hybrid seed now, there’s no point in saving old seed. I won’t deep-plough; I’ll direct-seed into the wheat stubble or do a very light pass to save time and keep moisture. I’ll apply compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress nitrogen at the big trumpet stage. Maize needs heat and water in July and August, so I’ll irrigate twice — at jointing/tasseling and at filling — and spray twice for weeds and corn borer. A good summer should give me a bit over 1,000 jin per mu.

I’m not chasing record yields. With only 1.5 mu and off-farm wages coming in, I want steady, low-risk production that doesn’t eat up all my labor or money on inputs.
